model.label: National Health Insurance: an earmarked income-related health tax plus general taxes, pooled by the National Insurance Institute and paid by risk-adjusted capitation to four competing non-profit health plans that both insure and deliver care; entitlement rests on residence, not on paying the tax

overview.statement: The Ministry of Health plans, regulates and enforces the system and also owns some facilities, while four competing health plans operating nationwide are responsible for delivering and paying for care (2024 review).

The health plans are independent non-profit bodies, first set up in the early twentieth century; since the 1995 National Health Insurance Law, coverage has been compulsory for all residents, who choose freely among the plans, may switch up to twice a year and cannot be refused.

National Health Insurance money comes from an earmarked income-related contribution (the health tax) plus general government funds; the National Insurance Institute collects and pools it and divides it among the plans by capitation adjusted for age, gender and place of residence.

Specialist care is mostly delivered by self-employed doctors in community clinics, while hospitals mainly provide imaging, inpatient and emergency care, reflecting a long-standing government policy of shifting care out of hospitals (2024 review).

The Ministry of Health and two municipalities own 45% of acute general hospital beds, the Clalit health plan owns 30%, non-governmental organisations 22%, and the Maccabi plan together with other for-profit owners 3% (2024 review).

financing.statement: As of January 2024 the health tax was charged on wages and other income in two bands: 3.1% of monthly income up to NIS 7,522 (60% of average monthly income) and 5% on income above that, up to a ceiling of NIS 49,030; every resident adult pays it except married women not working outside the home.
Adults with no income paid a flat health tax of NIS 116 a month (about EUR 20) as of January 2024.
An amendment to the 2024 state budget raised the health tax rates to 3.3% for the lower band and 5.2% for the upper band, with both increases due to apply from 2025, according to the WHO review.

In 2024, by the Central Bureau of Statistics national health expenditure accounts, 41.9% of health spending was funded from the state budget, 23% from the health tax, 33.7% from private sources and 1.4% from foreign donations.
Voluntary health insurance covered more than 89% of the population in 2022 and in 2021 paid for 10% of current health spending and 32% of private health spending (WHO health expenditure data).
Spending through voluntary health insurance was US$370 per person (PPP) in 2021, over twice the EU figure of US$171 and above the WHO European Region average of US$134.
Out-of-pocket payments fell from 29.5% of health spending in 2000 to 19.8% in 2021, close to the EU share (18.7%) but above the average for high-income countries in the WHO European Region (17.1%).

Foreign workers are outside the National Health Insurance and must hold private health insurance, two thirds paid by the employer and one third by the employee; they made up 1% of the population in 2021.

covered.statement: Entitlement to National Health Insurance benefits rests on permanent residence and enrolment in one of the four health plans, not on whether the person has paid the health tax.

The benefits package is an explicit positive list: it includes primary and secondary care, hospital inpatient care, diagnostic testing, rehabilitation and child development services, mental health care, and some dental care for children and older adults.

Each year new services and technologies are added to the package on the advice of a public interdisciplinary committee that weighs health technology assessment, including cost-effectiveness and budget impact; nothing is ever removed, and the covered medicines list is also updated annually.

Additions are approved by the Minister of Health on the recommendation of the 'benefits basket committee', whose members include health system representatives, the Ministry of Finance, clinicians, patients, religious groups and ethics and economics experts.
Adults are not covered for dental care unless they are 72 or older, and coverage of eye-care products such as glasses is limited.

The Ministry of Health can cover undocumented migrants' children and other children without a visa, with the same benefits as insured children, if their parents pay ILS 120 a month per child for up to two children; further children are covered free.

Health plans built their own information technology and digital services, such as electronic prescriptions and virtual visits, and all virtual services are included in National Health Insurance coverage.

cost_sharing.statement: Primary care visits (to GPs, paediatricians, gynaecologists and internal medicine specialists) cost nothing at the point of use, nor does hospital inpatient care; specialist visits carry fixed co-payments and medicines carry percentage co-payments of 15% of retail price for patented drugs and 10% for generics.
Under the WHO review's 2024 summary of user charges, the first visit to a given specialty in each calendar quarter costs NIS 22 to NIS 35 depending on the health plan.
People with chronic conditions have a monthly cap on medicine co-payments of NIS 298-315 depending on the plan, reduced to NIS 146-157.50 above retirement age (62 for women, 67 for men).
Every household has a separate cap on what it pays for specialist visits and diagnostic tests, but no single cap covers all user charges, and neither cap varies with income.

Patients on dialysis or treated for cancer, HIV/AIDS, Gaucher disease, cystic fibrosis, thalassemia, haemophilia or tuberculosis pay no user charges for visits, medicines and products related to those conditions; income-based exemptions generally apply only to people over 65.

The WHO review finds co-payment design weak: medicines carry percentage rather than fixed charges, the only income-based exemption is for specialist visit co-payments, and no cap covers all co-payments.

financial_hardship.statement: In 2022 catastrophic health spending was concentrated among poorer households: it affected 15% of households in the poorest consumption quintile and was above the national average among households headed by ultra-orthodox Jews (10%), older people (9%) and Arabs (7%).
Outpatient medicines and dental care drive catastrophic spending in the two poorest quintiles, while in richer quintiles dental care is the main driver, followed by medicines.

additional_care.statement: Household survey data show voluntary health insurance rising from about 79% of households in 2007 to about 89% in 2022; in 2022, 50% of households held only health-plan insurance, 38% held both health-plan and commercial policies, and 1% held only commercial cover.

Voluntary insurance sold by the health plans is regulated by the Ministry of Health and must accept all applicants, cover for life and vary premiums only by age; commercial policies are regulated more loosely by the Ministry of Finance and insurers may refuse applicants, price other policies by risk and end contracts.

Since 2015 no voluntary policy may pay National Health Insurance co-payments; commercial policies can cover treatment abroad and medicines outside the package, and since 2016 new commercial policies may no longer duplicate health-plan cover.

In national surveys in 2012 and 2022, about 83% of adults owned voluntary health insurance, but Arabs, residents of peripheral areas and people in the lowest income quintile were less likely to own it.
Self-reported use of voluntary insurance fell from 76% of owners in 2012 to 66% in 2022; specialist visits were the only service type whose use rose (from 20% to 28%).

access.statement: In 2020 the national median wait to see a specialist was 21 days, but 30 days in the Southern District.

Ministry of Health data show average community waits of about 50 days for endocrinology and neurology appointments, the longest among the specialties tracked, against about 20 days for orthopaedics and gynaecology (data to the first quarter of 2024).

In 2021 half of adults who went without publicly funded care because of waiting times got the care privately instead, a rate that was especially high among Arabs, higher earners and holders of voluntary insurance.
In 2021, 11% of adults aged 22 and over reported unmet needs for care or medicines because of cost, rising to 19% among adults with low incomes.
In 2023 Israel had 3.5 practising physicians per 1,000 people, below the OECD average of 3.9.
Israel had 5.57 practising nurses per 1,000 people in 2023, well below the OECD average of 9.5.

General hospital beds rose in number from 15,497 in 2015 to 16,948 in 2023 but fell per head, from 1.85 to 1.76 per 1,000 people, against an OECD average of 3.18 in 2023; psychiatric beds were 0.37 per 1,000 against an OECD average of 0.7.

Over 2021-2023 the national average was 5.4 employed nurses per 1,000 residents, with Tel Aviv (7.7) and Haifa (6.9) above it and the South (4.5), Jerusalem (4.8), Central (4.9) and Northern (5.2) districts below.

A Ministry of Health planning analysis found that 39% of cancer patients in the Southern District travel far from home for treatment, against 18% in the Haifa District and 12% in the Northern District.

outcomes.statement: OECD data for 2023 put life expectancy at birth in Israel at 83.8 years (85.7 for women, 81.7 for men), fourth among OECD countries after Switzerland, Japan and Spain.
In 2023 life expectancy was 80.7 years in the Arab population and 84.3 years in the Jewish population, excluding war casualties.
Infant mortality was 1.9 per 1,000 live births among Jews and others and 5.2 among Arabs, and twice the Arab rate among Bedouins.

Premature deaths at ages 30-69 from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes and chronic respiratory disease fell from 293 per 100,000 in 2000 to 156 in 2020, well under the latest WHO European Region (359, 2017) and EU (261, 2018) averages.
Excess mortality in Israel in both 2020 and 2021 was roughly a quarter of the WHO European Region average.
In the GBD 2019 study, Israel's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 83.1 (95% uncertainty interval 80.6-85.1) in 2019, 17.4 points higher than in 1990.

outcomes.statement: Diabetes affected 10.5% of adults aged 18 and over in 2023 and was 1.6 times as common in the Arab population as among non-Haredi and Haredi Jews.
Smoking has been increasing for years across population groups; in 2023, 29.3% of men and 13.7% of women smoked.

costs.statement: National health expenditure was NIS 146 billion in 2024, or 7.3% of GDP, below most OECD countries; current spending per person was US$3,941 at purchasing power parity, also lower than in most OECD countries.

Health spending per person was US$3,665 (PPP) in 2021, close to the WHO European Region average (US$3,841) but below the averages for the region's high-income countries (US$5,298) and the EU (US$4,733).
Public spending on health was 5.4% of GDP in 2021, under the EU and high-income country average of 7.1%.
In 2023 the public share of current national health spending (including the health tax) was low by OECD standards: only Mexico, Chile, Greece, Portugal and South Korea had lower shares.

The Taub Center chapter cites comparative research finding that Israel spends less on health than other developed systems, especially publicly, even after adjusting for age structure and long-term care, while achieving better outcomes.
In 2021, 41% of total health spending went to ambulatory primary and preventive care and 31% to hospitals and research.

what_works.statement: Despite low health spending per person and as a share of GDP, Israel outperforms the OECD average on 81% of the OECD's health status indicators, 78% of its risk factor indicators, 59% of quality of care indicators and 67% of access indicators, per OECD figures cited in the 2024 review.

verification.note: Statement copies 12+ consecutive words from the source; rewrite in own words.

what_works.statement: Primary care doctors coordinated care for 63% of adults aged 22 and over in 2021, supported by an electronic medical record that both clinicians and patients can access.
In 2021, 66% of people aged 22 and over looked at their own health records online, 55% contacted their plan or doctor through its website or app, and 44% consulted their doctor by video or chat.

The 1995 law deliberately separated contributions from entitlement so that no one loses cover for inability to pay and so that health plans cannot learn their members' incomes, which could otherwise encourage selection.

Israel's low COVID-19 mortality is attributed mainly to its rapid rollout of the first three vaccine doses, which reached a large share of the population very fast, partly by building on the health plans' primary care networks.

Among insured residents with mental health contact, community mental health visits rose fourfold and hospital outpatient psychiatric visits 3.3-fold after the 2015 transfer of mental health care to the health plans, with an adjusted 16% rise in service use over 2012-2019; emergency visits without admission also rose 40%.

In a 2025 comparison of five high-income systems, Israel had the highest life expectancy (82.6 years) and the lowest infant mortality (2.8 per 1,000) of the five, while spending 7.4% of GDP on health in 2022 against an OECD average of 9.2%.

After the February 2024 patient choice reform, travel distance to hospitals improved for Clalit and Meuhedet members; Clalit members in the periphery went from travelling about 11.3 km more than Maccabi members to 1.6 km more.

problems.statement: The physician-to-population ratio is projected to fall sharply in coming years because a quarter of physicians were over the retirement age of 67 in 2020.

Graduates of the foreign medical schools disqualified from 2025 by the Yatziv reform accounted for 51% of doctors working in the Negev and 63% in the Galilee in 2022, so the reform is expected to hit peripheral services hardest (State Ombudsman, 2024).

The WHO review finds that the very high take-up of supplementary insurance and of dual cover skews health resources towards richer households, so that lower-income households end up subsidising richer households' access.

Voluntary insurance pays private providers higher fees than the health plans do, pulling health workers away from public facilities, worsening shortages in the public sector and widening health inequities (2024 review, citing the Ministry of Health).
Higher public spending and higher spending through voluntary insurance have not lowered the share of households facing catastrophic health spending.

Refugees and asylum seekers who do not work and undocumented migrants, about 1% of the population, can use only publicly funded emergency care and some primary and specialist care for a few conditions.

After the 7 October 2023 attacks, demand for outpatient mental health care rose sharply; mental health care is covered, but long waits and high cost-sharing limit access and the understaffed public services struggled with the surge.
A measles outbreak from April 2025 led to 730 measles-related hospitalisations, mostly of children aged 1-4, and 12 deaths within under eight months.
A 2024 report found that only 66% of children aged 12-13 months had received a first measles vaccine dose (MMR/MMRV) by 13 months at family care centres.
In a 2022 national survey, 62% of respondents trusted the system to deliver appropriate care, but only 42% were confident their treatment costs would be covered.

reforms.statement: At the end of October 2025 the Ministry of Health introduced a new clinical training model for medical students, including unified payment for training places, training standards, central assignment of students and more training in community settings.
About 1,400 students started medicine at Israeli universities in the 2025-2026 academic year, a record and up from 731 in 2018; the Ministry of Health aims for 1,700 new students a year by 2030.

During the 2024 budget talks a differentiated increase in the health tax, to take effect in 2026, was proposed in connection with more investment in mental health care, though the Taub Center expects the extra revenue will probably not go directly to that purpose.
The Medical Information Mobility Law, approved in July 2024, provides for medical information to move quickly between health system organisations with the patient's consent.

In June 2024 holders of 'First Shekel' private policies were moved automatically to the health plans' supplementary 'Shaban' policies to end duplicate cover; the supplementary policy costs about 30% less, but premiums for those who stay in First Shekel were expected to rise about 45%.

A 2024 regulation requires commercial insurers to move customers who also hold health-plan insurance to policies covering only the gap between the actual cost of surgery and what the health-plan policy pays, and makes commercial insurers pay for private-hospital surgery for people with dual cover.

In 2024 physicians signed their first wage agreement in 13 years, with a 9.5% raise for all physicians and extra pay for national-priority fields such as mental health, rehabilitation and forensic medicine.

The Ministry of Health's 2023-2028 hospital bed plan first allocated 1,791 new beds; in 2024 it added 245 psychiatric and 300 rehabilitation beds for needs arising from the October 2023 attacks and the war.
From July 2023 the package added glasses for children under 8 (up to one pair a year), with maximum waits of 30 days for optometrist and ophthalmologist visits and 14 days for new glasses.

From July 2022 dental cover for people over 72 was widened to free preventive and restorative care, including root-end fillings, up to four implants to support a full lower denture, and specialist consultation.

The Yatziv reform, in force from 2019, disqualifies graduates of foreign medical schools it does not recognise, so that from 2025 many graduates will be unable to get an Israeli licence; the review expects this to reduce the number of new doctors substantially.
Free preventive and restorative dental care for children was extended step by step and reached all children under 18 in January 2019.

On 1 July 2015 responsibility and funding for mental health care moved from the Ministry of Health to the four health plans, to improve access, integrate mental and general care and shift care to the community.
In January 2015 co-payments for primary care visits (GPs, paediatricians and gynaecologists) were abolished.

us_lessons.statement: A 2025 five-country comparison concludes that higher spending does not guarantee quality: the US spends far more yet has lower life expectancy and higher avoidable mortality than Israel and the Netherlands, whose experience suggests strong results are possible at lower cost when systems are well organised.

The same comparison suggests that well-regulated social health insurance systems such as those of the Netherlands, Germany and Israel may balance equity, patient autonomy and performance better than loosely regulated private-market systems or highly centralised public ones.
